X.why: Strong hook: walking across the runway at midnight is vivid and neutral. The facts are concrete and checkable (14 sieges, only 5 changed hands, years and sources labelled). 'Told from both sides' records' reassures me it won't be a British flag-waver. Leading with a UK–EU treaty in the first seconds is a little political, but it's stated flatly.
X.moment_you_would_leave_or_doubt: 'Since July, under a new UK–EU treaty, there are no routine checks at this gate' — it is current-affairs framing and could be a lead-in to 'Spain is now cooperating', and I'd listen closely to the tone. The 'only five changed who ruled it' line could also be a hint that Spain mostly failed, if the narrator leans on it. The sources are all Anglo (Sayer, Gibraltar National Museum), so I'd doubt the 'both sides' promise until a Spanish source appears.

Y.why: The best at earning my trust fast. Putting Sayer next to Montero with the same 'key of the Mediterranean' image shows within seconds that Spanish sources get equal weight and that Spain is not the villain. It is clever, and it is respectful of Spanish historiography.
Y.moment_you_would_leave_or_doubt: 'Same rock. Same image. Opposite sides.' — a bit cute and it frames the whole thing as two rival stories, which risks a false equivalence on things like the Treaty of Utrecht. I'd doubt it if the Spanish quote turned out to be a token gesture and the rest relied on British sources. Also, no hard fact comes up until the fourteen-sieges card, so the hook is more about framing than content.

Z.why: A clean, punchy hook ('Fourteen.') and it promises the answer to the title right away. It says that British and Spanish historians count the same way, which is neutral. The two-column table of historians is a nice sign of balance.
Z.moment_you_would_leave_or_doubt: 'British and Spanish historians count the same way' is an unsupported claim stated before any names are shown, and I know the counts vary between authors, so I'd bristle slightly. 'Only five of those sieges changed who ruled it' with no context risks sounding like 'Spain kept failing'. The opening is generic, with a dark card and no emotional pull, so it is the easiest one to click away from.

one_change_to_the_best_version: Keep the Sayer/Montero pairing but add a hard fact to the beat after 'Opposite sides', e.g. 'Fourteen sieges, and only five changed hands', so the viewer gets substance as well as framing. Also make sure the Spanish quote is followed by a real Spanish account later, not just a one-line nod.
